Decision-focused contrast:

- Draft: content remains open to substantive change. Classification cue: substantive revision is still possible. Approved case: a memo awaiting author review. Nonexample: a memo formally released to staff.
- Published: content has been formally released to its intended audience. Classification cue: formal release to that audience. Approved case: an approved memo emailed to all staff. Nonexample: a memo saved privately.

Known confusion: Polished formatting is not a classification cue in either supplied definition. A polished document may still be a draft if substantive change remains open; formatting alone does not show formal release.

Suggested decision sequence: First ask whether the content was formally released to its intended audience. If yes, classify it as published. If not, ask whether it remains open to substantive change; if yes, classify it as a draft. A privately saved memo is not published, but the supplied facts alone do not establish that every unpublished item is a draft.

Either-or evidence assessment: The evidence does not support a universally exhaustive either-or question. The definitions distinguish the concepts, but they do not state that every document must be exactly one of them or that overlap is impossible. A sequential discriminating question is supported; forced binary classification is not.
